Abstract Forage yield, nutritive value, and stand persistence are key metrics in alfalfa ( Med- icago sativa L.) management. The combination of cultivar improvement, longer growing seasons in the Midwest, and trends of shorter alfalfa rotations offer oppor- tunity to reevaluate the effects of increasing cutting frequency (CF) on these met- rics. We evaluated forage yield, nutritive value, milk production, and persistence of eight alfalfa entries with fall dormancy (FD) ranging from two (FD2) to five (FD5) under CF of four (CF4), five (CF5), or six (CF6) annual cuts during two produc- tion years in two environments in the upper midwestern United States. Nutritive value and milk kg –1 alfalfa increased with increased CF and differed among alfalfa entries. Cutting frequency and alfalfa entry interactively influenced forage yield and milk production ha–1 yet optimal CF depended on environment. At one environment, increasing CF from CF4 to CF5 and from CF5 to CF6 caused a 5 and 29% decrease in milk ha–1, respectively. At another environment, CF5 had about 16% greater milk production than CF4 and CF6. The CF6 reduced persistence of 3rd-year stand density with the effects especially severe for some entries. Alfalfa entry FD was not corre- lated to forage yield or persistence, but an entry with FD5 was consistently among those with the greatest in forage and milk yield ha –1 at CF5 and CF6. These results suggest that intensifying CF from four to five harvests per season of some cultivars can boost yield and nutritive value without negative effects on stand persistence in some environments. 1 INTRODUCTION Maximizing yield of alfalfa ( Medicago sativa L.) forage with high nutritive value is a long-standing agronomic challenge. Forage nutritive value, which is often measured to establish a mon- etary value for alfalfa forage, declines with increasing alfalfa maturity resulting from decreased seasonal cutting frequency (CF) (Brink et al., 2010; Sheaffer et al., 1988; Undersander et al., 2010). In the Midwest, total season forage yields tend to increase up to three cuts per year but may decrease, remain Agrosyst Geosci Environ. 2022;5:e20246. wileyonlinelibrary.com/journal/agg2 1o f1 2 https://doi.org/10.1002/agg2.20246 [page 2] 2o f1 2 ECKBERG ET AL . the same, or increase with the fourth cutting (Brink & Marten, 1989; Grev et al., 2017; Sheaffer et al., 2000). Additional fall harvests, while increasing short-term seasonal yield, can result in reduced stand persistence during winters without adequate snow cover or when a period of warm weather dis- rupts dormancy (Brink & Marten, 1989; Sheaffer & Marten, 1990). Risk of yield reduction or winter injury from intensive harvest frequency increases with aging stands, declining soil fertility, pest pressure, and severe winter conditions (Jungers et al., 2019; Undersander et. al. et al., 2015). Therefore, pro- ducers should consider the tradeoffs among forage yield, for- age nutritive value, and stand persistence in developing prof- itable harvest systems for their farms. Recent advances in alfalfa breeding to improve alfalfa cul- tivar persistence may support intensification of harvest fre- quency in the Midwest (i.e., five or six annual harvests) that simultaneously improve forage yield and nutritive value. Modern cultivars with improved multiple disease resistance show superior stand persistence and yield under stressful envi- ronments (Lamb et al., 2006). Breeding and selection have also decoupled fall dormancy (FD) from winter hardiness leading to the development of less fall dormant alfalfa cul- tivars with both high regrowth potential and winter hardy rat- ings (Brummer et al., 2000; Lyons et al., 2016;N A F A ,2021). Modern cultivars developed for USDA Plant Hardiness Zones 2–6 are rated as FD4 (dormant) and FD5 (moderately dor- mant) may allow intensive harvest CF that push the upper limits of forage yield, nutritive value, and stand persistence. Ventroni et al. (2010), in Indiana, found that when evaluating three cultivars with FD 3, 6, and 10 subject to cutting fre- quencies of 20-, 30-, and 40-d intervals, cultivar FD had no effect on forage yield or stand persistence and that no culti- var× CF interaction occurred. However, this research did not include cultivars with intermediate FD 4 or 5, and additional research is needed on cultivars with FD levels typically used in the Upper Midwest. Alfalfa yield potential in Wisconsin and Minnesota is typ- ically reached during the first 2 yr of production, and Under- sander and Barnett ( 2008) recommended that maximum eco- nomic potential could be reached with alfalfa stand life short- ened to two production years. While some producers in Wis- consin and Minnesota do maintain stands only for 2 yr fol- lowing seeding, nearly 78% of stands are maintained from 3 t o6y r( Y o s te ta l . ,2014). Research on the performance of modern cultivars under intensive harvest regimes may illumi- nate certain combinations of cultivars and harvest frequencies adapted to shorter 2-yr alfalfa stands. Our objective was to evaluate six modern cultivars when subject to four, five or six- annual cuttings and test their interactive effects on forage yield and nutritive value and stand persistence over two production years. These cultivars were all high yielding and disease resis- tant and represented varying fall dormancy classes from 2 to 5. In addition to these commercial cultivars, we included two Core Ideas ∙ Alfalfa forage quality increased with increased cut- ting frequency. ∙ Alfalfa cultivars were affected differently across cutting frequencies. ∙ Alfalfa fall dormancy was not correlated to forage yield or persistence across cuttings. ∙ Intensifying cutting frequency from four to five harvests per season can increase yield. germplasm (USDA-ARS BIOMASS and USDA-ARS HIGH DIGEST; Lamb et al,2012;L a m be ta l ,2014) that were devel- oped for novel yield and nutritive value traits but that had not been evaluated under intensive harvest regimes. 2 MATERIALS AND METHODS Cutting frequency experiments were conducted from 2015 to 2017 on stands established in 2014 at Becker and St. Paul, MN. The soil at Becker, MN (45˚23 ′13″ N, 93˚53 ′18″ W, elevation 290 masl) was a Hubbard-Mosford complex (sandy, mixed, frigid Entic Hapludoll), and at St. Paul (44˚59′14″ N, 93˚10′24″ W, elevation 291 masl) the soil was a Waukegan silt loam (fine-silty over sandy or sandy-skeletal, mixed, superactive, mesic Typic Hapludoll). Air temperatures were similar among the two locations, but precipitation was slightly higher at Becker than at St. Paul (Table 1). Still, because of the low water holding capacity of the sandy soil at Becker, 14 cm of irrigation was applied each year at Becker. Soils were sampled (0–15 cm) and analyzed for available P, K, pH, and S at each site prior to planting and at each subse- quent fall. Fertilizers and lime were applied before secondary tillage and when soil testing indicated levels were below those recommended for at least 12.4 Mg ha–1 yr–1 of alfalfa produc- tion (Kaiser et al., 2011). Seed inoculated with appropriate alfalfa Rhizobium was planted into seedbeds with a Wintersteiger Plot seeder (Wintersteiger) at 18.8 kg ha−1 (pure live seed) in early May 2014. Plots were 1.8 by 6.1 m and weed control during the establishment year was a single application of ammonium salt of imazamox applied at 0.05 kg a.i. ha−1 (2-[4,5-dihydro- 4-methyl-4-(1-methylethyl)- 5-oxo-1 H-imidazol-2-yl]−5- (methoxymethyl)−3-pyridinecarboxylic acid). After the first alfalfa harvest in the seeding year, no further weed control was needed. The experimental design was a randomized complete block in a split-plot treatment arrangement with four replicates. Whole plot treatments include three CF treatments in the first and second production years (2015 and 2016) following seed- ing (2014) that provided a range of alfalfa maturity (Table 2). Cutting began 27 May each year and occurred at about 21-, 28-, and 45-d intervals before 1 September followed by a fall harvest about 1 October. This resulted in cutting treat- ments designated CF6, CF5, and CF4 to reflect six, five, and four cuts per year, respectively. Split-plot factors included eight alfalfa entries representing FD from 2.1 to 5 (designated entries 1 through 8): four cultivars from Alforex Seeds with FD 2.1, 3.4, 4.4, and 4.5; two from Pioneer Hi-Bred cultivars with FD 4 and 5 (designated entries 1–6, respectively; and two experimental populations (designated entry 7 and 8), USDA- ARS BIOMASS and USDA-ARS HIGH DIGEST, both with FD 3, based on FD of the parents. USDA-ARS BIOMASS and USDA-ARS HIGH DIGEST were selected for high yield and high stem digestibility, respectively (Lamb et al., 2012;L a m b et al., 2014). All alfalfa cultivars had medium to high levels of resistance to common diseases of alfalfa. During the seeding year, the first harvest of all alfalfa cul- tivars occurred 60 d after emergence and an additional har- vest occurred 45 d later where yield was assessed but it was not included in this analysis. Average seeding year yield was 3 . 5M gh a−1. No fall harvest occurred in the seeding year and stands for all cultivars were >95% ground cover with popula- tions >371 plants m−2. Forage yield was measured at each cutting by mechanically harvesting (Carter Manufacturing Co.) a 0.91 by 4 m area to a 5-cm height within the center of the plot. Bulk yield samples were weighed fresh and subsampled ( ∼0.5 kg). Subsamples were weighed fresh, then dried at 60 ˚C in a forced-air oven until constant weight to determine dry matter (DM) yield. To determine forage nutritive value and plant maturity, random duplicate samples were hand-harvested from a 0.1 m 2 area of each plot to a stubble height of 5 cm. Samples were immedi- ately weighed to determine wet weight. One subsample was dried at 60 ˚C and weighed for DM determination. The sub- sample was then ground in a Wiley mill (Thomas Scientific) to pass through a 6-mm screen followed by a 1-mm screen in a Cyclotec (Foss). Subsequent ground alfalfa samples were ana- lyzed for crude protein (CP), neutral detergent fiber (NDF), neutral detergent fiber digestibility (NDFD), and acid deter- gent fiber (ADF) using near infrared reflectance spectroscopy (NIRS) using a Perten NIRS (Model DA 7200; Perten Instru- ments) with calibration equations developed in Minnesota to estimate forage nutritive value. The standard error of cross validation was 0.98, 1.98, 1.52, and 2.64, respectively, for CP, ADF, NDF, and NDFD, while the R2 was .98, .80, .86, and .87, respectively. Relative forage quality (RFQ) was calculated and pre- sented in the following equation where the product of dry mat- ter intake (DMI) represented as a percentage of body weight (BW) and the total digestible nutrients divide by a scaler con- stant 1.23 (Undersander et al., 2010). RFQ =(DMI,%BW)(TDN,%DM)1.23 In addition to RFQ, milk production (i.e., MILK2006) was calculated using the University of Wisconsin Corn Silage Evaluation System (Shaver, 2006; Shaver et al., 2006). The other forage subsample from each plot was used to evaluate alfalfa maturity using the mean stage by count (MSC) method (Kalu & Fick, 1981) where vegetative growth included stages 0–2, budding included stages 3 and 4, and flowering included stages 5 and 6. In spring 2017, final forage yield was again measured using procedures previously described and plant densities were measured in two locations within each plot using a frequency grid (Vogel & Masters, 2001). Net returns were calculated by subtracting input costs from gross returns. Input costs were estimated using average prices for fuel, labor, and equipment depreciation associated with harvesting of forage using values provided by Lazarus ( 2009, 2011). Crop insurance, land costs, or interests on loans were not considered in production expenses. Gross returns were calculated by multiplying milk yield by average annual milk prices for Minnesota using the Mailbox milk price generated by the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service. Average milk prices were US$0.385 kg−1 in 2015 (USDA AMS, 2015) and $0.358 kg−1 in 2016 (USDA AMS, 2016). 3 Statistical analysis All data were analyzed using the statistical program R. Cut- ting frequency, alfalfa entries, and their interaction were tested with analysis of variance (α= .05) using linear mixed effects models (lme) which included random effects for block and whole plot (CF) nested within block to accommodate a split design. Pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means were made using Tukey HSD (Lenth, 2019). Correlations among maturity rating, FD, yield, and nutritive value response variables were tested using Pearson’s correlation test. Results for all variables are presented as an average over the two pro- duction years following seeding because we focused on the effect of use of alfalfa in short-term rotations. Results are pre- sented separately for Becker and St. Paul, MN, because of the uniqueness in environments and soils. 4 RESULTS AND DISCUSSION 4.1 Alfalfa maturity and forage yield F o rB e c k e r(F = 361.5, numerator degrees for freedom [ndf] = 2, denominator degrees for freedom [dfd] = 797, P < .001) and St. Paul ( F = 256.5, ndf = 2, dfd = 573, P < .001), the effect of CF on MSC was significant. At Becker and St. Paul, increasing CF from CF4 to CF6 reduced alfalfa maturity at harvest. Maturity (MSC) for CF4, CF5, and CF6 was 5.0, 3.1, and 1.5, respectively, at Becker; and 5.5, 3.8, and 2.3, respectively, at St. Paul. These differences in matu- rity within locations were expected because the 45-d harvest interval for the CF4 treatment allowed the alfalfa more time to mature than for CF5 and CF6 which had about a 28- and 21-d harvest interval, respectively (Table 2). Alfalfa entries had similar maturity despite difference in FD reaction. Typically, over the wide range of alfalfa cultivar FD, less dormant alfalfa cultivars mature quicker than more dormant cultivars (Lyons et al., 2016; Ventroni et al., 2010). In our study, the range of FD may not have been enough to cause differences in maturity (correlation coefficient = .03, P = .60). Greater maturity at St. Paul using the same cal- endar date scheduling was likely due to slightly warmer air temperatures at St. Paul than at Becker (Table 1). These results also reaffirm the recommendation for use of crop maturity for scheduling alfalfa cutting rather than calendar date or time between cuttings to best predict alfalfa yield and nutritive value as a function of crop development (Sheaffer et al., 1988). Bars indicate ± 1 standard error treatment and alfalfa entry significantly influenced forage yields at both locations (Table 3, Figure 1). Based on differences in average maturity at harvest, we expected to observe the greatest yields for CF4 and the low- est for CF6 (Undersander et al., 2015). At both locations, the CF6 treatment had the lowest alfalfa forage yield but changes in yield with increasing CF from CF4 to CF5 were not con- sistent between locations (Table 4). At Becker, increasing CF from CF4 to CF5, and CF5 to CF6 deceased yields 16 and 34%, respectively; but at St. Paul, average yields increased 11% from CF4 to CF5 but decreased 24% from CF5 to CF6. This increased yield at St. Paul from CF5 compared to CF4 may have been due to yield gained from the additional late- summer to early-fall cutting for the CF5 treatment that com- pensated for the forage yield associated with the lower average seasonal maturity compared to CF4. Averaged over all cutting treatments, entry 6 was consis- tently among the greatest yielding at both locations, but the relative yield ranking for the other alfalfa entries was not con- sistent over locations (Table5). The cutting treatment× alfalfa entry interaction showed that there were greater differences in yield among CF5 and CF6 compared to CF4 (Figure 1). Alfalfa entry 6 was consistently among the greatest yielding at all cutting treatments. Entry 6 had one of the greatest FD ratings (FD 5) which may have contributed to greater regrowth potential and improved total season yield for all CF; how- ever, it was not more mature than the other entries at har- vest. Averaged for all CF, entry FD level was not a strong pre- dictor for alfalfa entry differences in forage yield (correlation coefficient = .07; P = .39). To further evaluate the effect of FD on forage yield, we compared the yield of entry 1 (FD2) and entry 6 (FD5) at individual cuttings (Figure 2). Although entry 6 did appear to have greater yields than entry 1 at some cuttings, these differences were only statistically significant at the fourth cutting of CF4 and the fifth cutting of CF5 at Becker, and the fifth cutting of CF6 at St. Paul. Our results for entries within the FD2–FD5 range contrast with the idea that the fall acclimation response limits forage DM production, and that cultivars with higher FD ratings have potential for higher forage yields than more dormant cultivars (Brummer et al., 2000; Lyons et al., 2016). The USDA-ARS BIOMASS (entry 7) was selected for use in an infrequent two- or three- cut biofuel production system (Lamb et al., 2012); therefore, its poor forage yield relative to the other cultivars with CF5 and CF6 is not surprising. Our results agree with previous research (e.g., Brink & Marten, 1986; Brink et al., 2010; Kallenbach et al., 2002; Ventroni et al., 2010) that showed it is possible to identify a CF in specific environments that optimizes yield. In Min- nesota, research conducted over 28 yr ago showed that cutting three times at a 45-d interval plus the fall produced greater DM yields than systems with three or four cuts at 45- and 30-d intervals, respectively, before early September (Brink & Marten, 1989; Sheaffer & Marten, 1990). We observed high yield potential at St. Paul using modern cultivars under both CF4 and CF5. Our study suggests modern cultivars may have increased productivity under a CF5 in some environments if maturity is approaching early to late bud, but research is needed across more environments to verify this observation. 4.2 Forage nutritive value Increased CF from CF4 to CF6, which was associated with less maturity at harvest, increased average season forage CP [page 6] 6o f1 2 ECKBERG ET AL .
